title: 132 Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every triple versus a monotonic stack scanning right to left that tracks the best possible completion.

blocks.text: Given an array of n integers nums, a "132 pattern" is a subsequence of THREE integers nums[i], nums[j], nums[k] such that i < j < k AND nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]. Return true if there is a 132 pattern anywhere in nums, otherwise return false.

blocks.caption: Walking right to left with a monotonic stack of "3" candidates and a running "best 2 found so far" resolves the search in one pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of integers nums"],["Output","True if a valid i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] exists, false otherwise"],["Goal","Detect a 132 pattern in a single linear pass, without checking every possible triple"],["Constraints","1 <= nums.length <= 2*10^5; -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A specific ORDERED relationship among three positions (the middle one, nums[j], must be the LARGEST) is being searched for","A monotonic stack, tracking candidates for the \"peak\" (nums[j], the \"3\") while scanning"],["The search benefits from knowing \"the best possible middle value\" as early as possible","Scanning RIGHT TO LEFT lets each position act as a candidate \"1\" (nums[i]), checked against an already-computed best \"2\" (nums[k]) found from everything to its right"]]}

blocks.text: A "132 pattern" needs three positions in increasing index order where the FIRST value is the smallest, the MIDDLE value is the largest (the "peak"), and the LAST value is strictly between them; the name comes from "1" (smallest), "3" (largest, in the middle position), "2" (in between, at the end).

blocks.title: Analogy: A Small Dip, Then a Tall Peak, Then a Medium Landing
blocks.text: Imagine a hiking trail's elevation profile: starting LOW, climbing to a TALL peak, then descending to a MEDIUM elevation (higher than the start, but lower than the peak). This exact shape (low, then a peak, then a medium landing) is what a 132 pattern looks for anywhere within the sequence of elevations, not necessarily consecutively.

blocks.caption: A right-to-left scan lets a running "best confirmed nums[k] candidate" (third) be checked against every earlier candidate nums[i] in a single pass

blocks.text: Before checking every possible triple directly (an O(n^3) brute force), notice that scanning RIGHT TO LEFT while maintaining "the best possible nums[k] candidate found so far" lets each position be checked as a potential nums[i] against an already-optimized target.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Scanning from the RIGHT means that by the time a position is reached, everything to its right (potential nums[j] and nums[k] pairs) has already been fully processed.

Observation 2: Maintaining a monotonic stack of "3" (nums[j], peak) candidates, where a NEW, bigger value encountered while scanning right-to-left can "dominate" (pop) smaller stack entries, each dominated entry becomes a candidate for "2" (nums[k]), since it is smaller than the value that just dominated it (a valid nums[j] > nums[k] relationship).

Observation 3: Tracking the BEST (largest) such "2" candidate found so far in a single variable (third) means: the moment a NEW position's value is found to be SMALLER than third, a full valid 132 pattern has been found, since third is guaranteed to have a corresponding, even LARGER "3" value still sitting on the stack (or having just been popped) further to the right.

Observation 4: This single right-to-left pass, combined with the monotonic stack and the running "third" variable, checks every position as a potential nums[i] against the BEST possible completion, all in O(n) total.
This is a monotonic stack technique scanning right to left: track the best "2" (nums[k]) candidate confirmed so far, and check each new position against it as a potential "1" (nums[i]).
Directly check every possible triple of indices i < j < k, verifying whether nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j] holds for any of them.

items: Try every combination of three indices i < j < k using three nested loops.
Return true the moment any triple satisfies nums[i] < nums[k] < nums[j]; return false if no such triple exists after checking all of them.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Three nested loops directly implement the definition, checking every possible ordered triple exhaustively.
This guarantees correctness (nothing is missed), but at a steep computational cost.

blocks.text: Always correctly finds a valid 132 pattern if one exists, since every possible triple is explicitly checked.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^3), checking every triple of indices.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: O(n^3) is far too slow for the given constraints (up to 2*10^5 elements); a monotonic stack scanning right to left resolves the same question in O(n) time.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force checks every triple explicitly. Instead, scan RIGHT TO LEFT, maintaining a monotonic stack of "3" (peak) candidates and a running "third" variable holding the best "2" (nums[k]) value confirmed so far. For each position (treated as a potential "1"), first check if its value is smaller than "third" (an immediate pattern match); otherwise, pop any smaller stack entries into "third" (they are dominated, becoming new "2" candidates), then push the current value as a new "3" candidate.

Initialize an empty stack and third = negative infinity. Walk nums from right to left. For each value: if it is less than third, return true immediately. Otherwise, while the stack is non-empty and its top is less than the current value, pop it and set third to that popped value. Push the current value onto the stack. If the loop completes without finding a match, return false.
Scan right to left with a monotonic stack of "3" candidates, tracking the best "2" candidate confirmed so far.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step (right to left)","Value","Action","Stack after","third after"],"rows":[["1st","2","2 < -inf? No. Push 2","[2]","-inf"],["2nd","4","4 < -inf? No. Pop 2 (2<4): third=2. Push 4","[4]","2"],["3rd","1","1 < third(2)? YES: 132 pattern found!","-","-"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The value 1 (as nums[i]) is less than third=2 (nums[k], which was dominated by nums[j]=4, still available further right), confirming a valid 132 pattern, matching the expected true result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each element is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

When a stack entry is popped because a new, bigger value dominates it, that popped entry becomes a confirmed valid "2" (nums[k]) candidate, since a bigger "3" (nums[j] = the new value) exists to its right that is greater than it. Tracking the LARGEST such confirmed "2" candidate in "third" maximizes the chance a LATER (further left) position can be smaller than it, satisfying nums[i] < nums[k]. The moment such a position is found, all three pieces (a valid nums[j] > third, still implicitly available; third itself as nums[k]; and the current position as nums[i]) are confirmed to exist in the correct index order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["The current value is less than third","A complete 132 pattern is confirmed immediately: return true"],["The current value dominates (is bigger than) the stack's top","That top entry becomes the new best \"2\" candidate (third), and popping continues"],["The current value does not dominate the top","It is simply pushed as a new \"3\" candidate for future (further left) positions to potentially find a pattern against"]]}

items: Checking "num < third" BEFORE any stack popping ensures the CURRENT (not yet updated) best "2" candidate is used, correctly reflecting everything confirmed so far to the right.
The while loop update of "third" always keeps it as the MOST RECENTLY dominated (and therefore typically largest useful) "2" candidate, maximizing future match potential.
Scanning strictly right to left (not left to right) is essential, since the algorithm relies on having ALREADY processed everything to the right of the current position before checking it.

blocks.text: Detecting a specific three-part ORDERED pattern (small, then peak, then medium) in an array can often be resolved in O(n) using a monotonic stack combined with a single "best candidate found so far" variable, scanning in the direction that lets that variable be USED immediately as new positions are checked.

items: Scanning left to right instead of right to left, which would not have the necessary "everything to the right already processed" information available when checking each position.
Checking "num < third" AFTER updating third (using the stack-popping loop) rather than BEFORE, incorrectly using information that should not yet apply to the current position.
Attempting to track the actual nums[j] value explicitly, when only the best possible nums[k] (third) ever needs to be tracked for the check to work correctly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Array length less than 3","No valid triple can exist, so the result is always false"],["A strictly increasing array","No position can ever be a valid \"peak\" (nums[j]) with something smaller after it, so the result is false"],["Negative numbers present","Handled correctly, since \"third\" is initialized to negative infinity and all comparisons work identically regardless of sign"]]}

items: Explicitly explaining why scanning RIGHT TO LEFT (rather than the more common left-to-right direction) is necessary here demonstrates careful attention to exactly what information the algorithm needs available at each step.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find a specific ORDERED three-element pattern (especially with the middle element as an extreme/peak)" points toward a monotonic stack, often combined with a single running "best candidate" variable.

items: How would you find ALL such 132 pattern triples, not just detect whether one exists? The same right-to-left scan could be adapted to record every (i, third) match found, rather than returning immediately on the first one.

How does this problem's technique compare to Next Greater Element I? Both use a monotonic stack, but this problem additionally tracks a SEPARATE running variable (third) capturing information about POPPED elements, rather than just resolving direct matches.

Why does the algorithm only need to track the BEST (not all) "2" candidates? Because a LARGER "third" value is strictly easier for a future (further left) nums[i] to be smaller than, making it the most useful single candidate to retain.

A more advanced monotonic stack technique building on Next Greater Element I and Daily Temperatures, here additionally tracking information about POPPED elements (not just resolving direct next-match queries).

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^3) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (monotonic stack, right to left): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic stack scanning right to left, tracking the best "dominated" candidate

Core Idea: Scan right to left; a monotonic stack of "3" (peak) candidates pops smaller entries into a running "best 2 (nums[k]) found so far" variable, and any position smaller than that variable confirms a full 132 pattern
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Only the LARGEST confirmed "2" candidate needs to be tracked, since it is the easiest target for a future smaller value to beat
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Right to left; pop smaller stack values into "third"; if current < third, a 132 pattern exists
